Patient-reported symptoms:

  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Vignette:
The sky had turned that bruised green before the sirens even finished wailing, but Julian Vance only remembers the exact second the tin roof of his childhood bedroom groaned and gave way. Rain lashed sideways, carrying the sharp, metallic tang of ozone and splintered cedar. Shards of glass rained onto his mattress as the wind screamed through the shattered window, and for three agonizing minutes, Julian lay pressed against the floorboards, certain the ceiling would follow. When the roar finally faded to a dull, dripping silence, he climbed out into a yard buried under fallen branches and standing water. The smell of wet concrete, gasoline, and damp insulation clung to everything. He had come to believe that the ground could shift without warning, a certainty that now lived in his chest like a coiled spring. In the weeks that followed, Julian found himself trapped in a loop of visual fragments. Closing his eyes no longer brought rest; instead, it summoned crisp, unblinking images of splintered drywall and the way the streetlamp had flickered once before dying. The more he pressed his palms to his temples or focused intently on his phone screen, trying hard not to think about the storm, the more insistently the memories returned. Worse was the smell. When a summer storm rolled in or a delivery truck sprayed the curb, the scent of wet asphalt and burnt wiring would hit him, and the terror he felt at the time would flood back, identical to the panic that had once pinned him to the floor. What frightened him most was not the memory itself, but the sudden, suffocating certainty that the sky was about to fall again. Julian took a job at the burger chain on Elm Street hoping routine would ground him, but the kitchen quickly became a place where he monitored every shift. The lunch rush required split-second decisions, shouted ticket orders, and a constant stream of demanding voices. He found himself standing behind the fry station, rehearsing what to say before any interaction: the exact words he would use to hand over a tray, the polite phrase he would offer if an order was wrong, the careful steps to avoid making a mistake. He had come to believe that any unexpected demand could spiral into chaos he could not control. He also began avoiding anything that could be stressful. He declined extra hours, left exactly at his scheduled time, and would step out to the back alley whenever the hood vents grew too loud. Over months, these patterns simply co-existed with his daily routine. His manager stopped assigning him to register duty, and a senior cook quietly noted that Julian no longer participated in team breaks, preferring to eat alone in his truck. The distance between who he was and who he felt he had become grew wider with each passing week. At nineteen, looking in the bathroom mirror, Julian barely recognized the hollow-eyed face staring back. The person he had become was unrecognizable to him. He used to be a happy person who laughed at his friends’ jokes and planned summer trips with his cousins; now, he is always miserable, and a heavy, unshakable dread settles over him the moment he wakes up. He was certain that he had permanently changed for the worse, that the bright, reckless teenager he used to be was gone. Friends texted less often, and he never replied, too exhausted from the daily work of holding his thoughts down and scanning the room. He had told himself he would just ride it out, but the exhaustion was becoming too much. Last Tuesday, after a sudden gust of wind rattled the service door and sent a familiar jolt of terror through his ribs, he finally walked into the community health clinic on 4th Street. He did not know if he could ever feel happy again, but he was hoping someone might help him understand why he felt so fundamentally broken.
